newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Mobutu boosts hopes of saving refugees in Zaire.
newsitem.headline: Mobutu boosts hopes of saving refugees in Zaire.

text.p: Prospects for an intervention force to save 1.2 million stranded war refugees in eastern Zaire look more likely after an all-clear from the country's ruler.
Ailing President Mobutu Sese Seseko backed the French initiative in talks with special U.N. envoy Raymond Chretien at his retreat in southern France on Wednesday.
Tutsi rebels who have overwhelmed the Zaire army in two eastern provinces oppose France's participation in the force.
With no other major power willing or able to deploy rapidly, it is uncertain whether the U.N. Security Council will give its blessing to a plan likely to be dominated by Paris.
Senior U.S. officials said on Wednesday that Washington was leaning toward backing the proposed force but would not itself contribute ground troops.
State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns told reporters Washington is reviewing all proposals put forward.
"Some of the proposals would require logistical support by the United States Armed Forces. We're not talking about ground force units (but) logistical support. And we're looking at that question."

Eight African countries, including Rwanda which is accused by Zaire of joining the rebels, backed the idea of a "neutral" force at talks in Nairobi on Tuesday. They did not define neutral, but neither did they specifically exclude anyone.
Chretien told reporters Mobutu endorsed proposals for a multinational force to get relief to the refugees from Rwanda and Burundi and help them return home.

"President Mobutu told me Zaire would do everything possible to maintain this period of calm so that the multinational force discussed in Nairobi may be able to rapidly allow for food to reach refugees and help them return to their home countries, including of course Rwanda," said Chretien, a Canadian diplomat.
"He was very clear, very categorical," Chretien said after the half-hour meeting at Mobutu's French Riviera villa.

There was no mention of Zaire's earlier statement that aid agencies should not distribute food aid on its soil. Information Minister Boguo Makeli said distribution should take place in Rwanda and Burundi to encourage refugees to go home.

Banyamulenge Tutsis battling the army declared a temporary truce on Monday which appears to be holding. But aid workers have had little news of the Hutu refugees dispersed from their camps by fighting.

Most are Rwandan Hutus who fled violence in their homeland in 1994. They fear vengeance at home for the massacre of up to a million minority Tutsis or their sympathisers by hardline Hutus that year. Tutsis went on to win the civil war and are in power.

The influx of Hutu refugees into eastern Zaire stoked rivalries in the area where Banyamulenge Tutsis settled from Rwanda 200 years earlier. Tutsis took up arms in their Mulenge Mountains stronghold after the army's attempts to expel them.

France, Spain and Ethiopia have offered troops for a force of about 5,000 initially proposed by France. Paris has said it wanted all major countries to participate and the force should be rapidly replaced by African troops.
French Foreign Minister Herve de Charette voiced disappointment at the lack of response, blaming it on "the international community's spinelessness".
"I'm knocking on doors, asking if anyone is prepared to assume his responsibilities. The answer is 'could you come back tomorrow?'" de Charette told LCI television.
The 66-year-old Zairean president, who has been away from Zaire since August undergoing treatment for prostate cancer, earlier made a brief appearance before a handful of reporters.
Wearing an elegant black and white jacket, he briefly chatted with a French TF1 television crew. TF1 said Mobutu looked tired but his voice was well assured.
Chretien was due to go on to Kinshasa for talks with Zaire's Prime Minister Kengo wa Dondo, a part-Tutsi who is target of angry demonstrators accusing him of being soft on the rebellion.

A Tutsi witch-hunt in the capital spread to the northeastern provincial town of Kisangani where students burned Tutsi-owned property. Nearly 1,000 Tutsis have fled Kinshasa to neighbouring Congo and many are missing or in hiding, Tutsis say.
